catalog_quote: The available data suggests that Tajio does not have lexical (word) stress; rather, it has a phrasal accent. Without lexical stress, the presence of the pitch accent depends on the location of the syllable within the intonational phrase. In words uttered in isolation, the penultimate syllable is regularly prominent. But, this does not mean that all words are stressed on the penultimate syllable. Rather, a phrasal accent regularly occurs on this syllable, because it is the penultimate syllable of an intonational phrase (i.e., it is auditorily prominent because a pitch rise associated with intonational phrases occurs on it). ... new_statements.quote: Stress is usually not indicated, since it regularly falls on the penultimate syllable in all Tomini-Tolitoli languages. Only the exceptions to this rule are marked. Primary stress is marked by an acute accent <'>, secondary stress (i.e. lengthening of reduplicated syllables) by a grave accent <`>. Most exceptions to the general stress rule are well-motivated (either a phonetically long vowel is shortened (cf. §3.4.6 above) or stress moves to the first member of a sequence of unlike vowels as in taipang 'mango', which occurs as an alternate to the regular taipang). In Balaesang, however, stress also occurs on final short closed syllables as in moontol [montól] 'sharp'. (p. 73; the acute marks on the two taipang forms are not preserved in the PDF text layer)
new_statements.citation: Himmelmann, Nikolaus P. 2001. Sourcebook on Tomini-Tolitoli languages. Pacific Linguistics 511. Canberra: ANU.
new_statements.locator: sec. 3.4.8 'Stress', printed p. 73 (PDF page 95 of 458); see also sec. 3.4.7 paragogic vowels p. 72, sec. 3.5.10 reduplication p. 81, sec. 3.8.2 possessive suffixes vs clitics pp. 91-92
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog holds a Tajio record with an empty rule and no existing statements; this source supplies the placement (penultimate) plus the suffix/clitic and paragogic-vowel conditions. Tajio-specific caveats: the general statement covers all Tomini-Tolitoli languages at once, and the author notes (p. 40, sec. 2.3) that Tajio data were collected at one location only (Sienjo).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls regularly on the penultimate syllable of the phonological word in every Tomini-Tolitoli language, Tajio included; the word lists mark only deviations. Suffixes (all monosyllabic but one) count toward the word and shift stress rightward onto the stem-final syllable, whereas clitics and free pronouns do not (pp. 91-92). Paragogic vowels added to consonant-final words in the northern Tomini languages do not attract stress, so such words surface with antepenultimate stress (p. 72). Tajio is discussed in this section only as one of the northern Tomini languages; the final-closed-syllable exception is explicitly restricted to Balaesang.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress = the lengthened reduplicated syllable of 'accented (C)CV-reduplication' (RDP1), marked with a grave accent; speakers vary in how strongly it is realised (sec. 3.5.10, p. 81).
new_statements.exceptions: (a) shortened phonetically long vowels; (b) stress on the first member of a sequence of unlike vowels (táipang ~ taípang 'mango'); (c) paragogic vowels leave stress in place, giving surface antepenultimate stress (Lauje lúba'E 'hair'); (d) enclitics do not shift stress, suffixes do; (e) Balaesang only: final short closed syllables can bear stress; (f) Lauje only: after final vowel deletion in clitics/suffixes stress stays on the now-final syllable (p. 81); (g) Boano only: some possessed forms with antepenultimate stress (fn. 34, p. 92).
new_statements.identity_note: Himmelmann 2001 describes Tajio (Kasimbar) as one of the northern Tomini languages of the Tomini-Tolitoli group, with Tajio word-list data from one village (Sienjo, Kecamatan Ampibabo); the stress statement is made once for the whole Tomini-Tolitoli group, and the exceptions singled out for Balaesang, Lauje and Boano do not concern Tajio. Himmelmann & Kaufman 2020 is not about Tajio at all.

readall_conflicts: Between the two listed works there is no conflict: Himmelmann 2001 states regular penultimate stress for all Tomini-Tolitoli languages including Tajio, and Himmelmann & Kaufman 2020 never mentions Tajio (its general caution that impressionistic penultimate-stress claims in Austronesian may really be phrase-level prominence applies in principle but is not directed at Tajio). One disagreement exists with a Tajio-specific source already held by the project but not in this works list: Mayani 2015/2016 (Linguistik Indonesia 34(1): 67-83, 'Phrasal accent in Tajio', file, scanned text) argues on acoustic grounds that 'Tajio does not have lexical (word) stress; rather, it has a phrasal accent. Without lexical stress, the presence of the pitch accent depends on the location of the syllable within the intonational phrase. In words uttered in isolation, the penultimate syllable is regularly prominent' (scanned p. 78-79). So the placement (penultimate prominence in isolation) agrees, but the type differs: Himmelmann 2001 = penultimate word stress; Mayani = no word stress, phrase-level pitch accent on the penult of the intonational phrase. The catalog should record the penultimate placement with this type dispute noted.

audit.reasoning: The classification (no-word-stress; phrase-level H accent on the IP-penultimate syllable, shifting under suffixation and absent on non-final words) rests on the language's only reference grammar (Mayani 2013, 208 pp), which we hold; the deciding quotation and the domain quotation are verbatim at the stated locators (sec. 2.7 pp. 46-48; sec. 3.1.1; sec. 1.4). The section is instrumentally supported (F0 tracks) and argues the stress-vs-accent distinction explicitly. The author's 2015/2016 Linguistik Indonesia article, downloaded now and scanned-read (pp. 79-82), repeats the analysis word for word, so two primary sources agree.
